concepts.title: CHAR versus VARCHAR Storage
concepts.definition: CHAR(n) reserves room for exactly n characters and pads shorter entries with trailing spaces, while VARCHAR(n) only caps the length and stores just the characters actually typed. Choosing VARCHAR over CHAR for short entries in a wide table therefore saves the padding on every single row.
concepts.key_idea: Fixed width pays for the padding on every row; variable width pays only for what is typed.
question_patterns: how many bytes does CHAR(10) occupy for the value 'city' and why
a CHAR(10) city column and a VARCHAR(30) alternative both hold 4-character names across 200 rows; how many bytes does VARCHAR save

solution_steps.action: size the fixed-width column over the table
solution_steps.explain: CHAR pads every row to the declared width, so rows times width gives its cost
VARCHAR stores only the typed characters on each row
the padding removed from every row is the difference between the two costs

concepts.title: MySQL Data Types and Constraints
concepts.definition: Every column gets a data type: INT for whole numbers (4 bytes each, BIGINT 8), FLOAT for decimals (4 bytes), DATE for calendar values written as yyyy-mm-dd, CHAR and VARCHAR for text. Constraints then police the values: NOT NULL forbids blanks, UNIQUE forbids repeats, DEFAULT supplies a fallback, PRIMARY KEY identifies each row, and FOREIGN KEY points at another table's key.
concepts.key_idea: Types decide what a column can hold, constraints decide what it must obey; together they keep data reliable.

solution_steps.action: match the data to a type
solution_steps.explain: whole counts take INT, measured values FLOAT, calendar days DATE, text CHAR or VARCHAR
NOT NULL and UNIQUE block blanks and duplicates; DEFAULT fills an omitted value
PRIMARY KEY tags each row uniquely; FOREIGN KEY references another table's primary key

concepts.title: DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, DESCRIBE
concepts.definition: Structure is managed with the Data Definition Language: CREATE DATABASE and CREATE TABLE build the containers, USE selects the active database, DESCRIBE (or DESC) prints a table's columns and types, ALTER TABLE adds, modifies or drops columns and constraints, and DROP removes a table or whole database permanently and irreversibly.
concepts.key_idea: CREATE builds, DESCRIBE inspects, ALTER adjusts structure, DROP destroys without any undo.

solution_steps.explain: the database first, then its tables with typed columns, then USE to activate it
DESCRIBE lists each column's type, nullability and key role
ALTER reshapes a table in place; DROP erases the table or database for good

concepts.title: DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
concepts.definition: Rows are maintained with three statements: INSERT INTO puts new records in, naming columns explicitly when only some values are known; UPDATE ... SET rewrites existing values and must carry a WHERE clause to spare the other rows; DELETE FROM removes matching rows, and omitting its WHERE clause wipes the entire table.
concepts.key_idea: Insert adds rows, update edits them, delete removes them; without WHERE the last two hit every row.
question_patterns: write the INSERT statement to add a guardian row where GPhone is not known

solution_steps.explain: values line up with the columns, or with the listed column names when some are skipped
UPDATE changes only the rows the WHERE condition selects
DELETE drops the selected rows; a forgotten WHERE condition empties the table

concepts.title: Annual Salary Computed Column
concepts.definition: A SELECT list may hold arithmetic on columns, not just raw columns: multiplying the pay column by 12 produces each employee's yearly figure, and the keyword AS renames the computed output for display. Such a calculated column exists only in the query result and never becomes a stored column.
concepts.key_idea: Arithmetic inside the SELECT list computes per row; AS only relabels the output column.

concepts.title: Net Profit of Movies
concepts.definition: Two stored columns can be subtracted inside a query to yield a business answer: for each movie, the net profit is the business cost minus the production cost, and expressing that profit as a percentage of the production cost shows the return margin. For an unreleased movie both figures are unknown, so the computed result stays unknown too.
concepts.key_idea: Business cost minus production cost gives the profit row by row; divide by the production cost for the margin percent.

solution_steps.action: subtract the cost from the earnings
solution_steps.explain: business cost minus production cost leaves the profit for that movie

solution_steps.action: express the profit as a margin
solution_steps.explain: dividing the profit by the production cost and scaling by 100 gives the return percentage

concepts.title: Department Salary Aggregate
concepts.definition: A WHERE clause can first filter the rows of one department, and the filtered salaries can then be totalled or averaged exactly as in arithmetic: add the selected figures, then divide by how many employees were selected. For the chapter's EMPLOYEE table, department D01 holds the salaries 60000, 45000 and 15000.
concepts.key_idea: Filter first with WHERE, then sum the surviving values and divide by their count for the department average.

dividing the department total by its employee count gives the mean salary

concepts.title: DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIKE and NULL Refinement
concepts.definition: Query output is polished with four tools: DISTINCT strips repeated values from a column, ORDER BY arranges rows ascending by default or descending with DESC, LIKE matches text patterns using percent for any run of characters and underscore for exactly one, and IS NULL or IS NOT NULL tests for missing values, since comparing against NULL with equals never works.
concepts.key_idea: DISTINCT de-duplicates, ORDER BY sorts, LIKE patterns with % and _, and only IS NULL finds blanks.
question_patterns: which clause removes duplicate values from the output of a query
write the query that lists employees in descending order of salary
which query lists employees whose names start with the letter K
what does the underscore wildcard represent in a LIKE pattern
write the condition to fetch employees who have not been given a bonus

how many rows does the query SELECT DISTINCT DeptId FROM EMPLOYEE return

solution_steps.explain: DISTINCT collapses repeats; ORDER BY sequences rows, with DESC reversing the default ascending order
LIKE pairs percent (any run of characters) and underscore (one character) to find substrings
NULL means unknown, so IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are the only valid checks

worked_examples.q: Which keyword strips repeated values from output?

solution_template.explain: 200 * 10 = 2000 bytes with padding on every row
